question.en: Why should you prefer semantic HTML over styled div elements?

answer.en:
Semantic elements communicate purpose, not just appearance. A `button` supplies keyboard activation and a native role; `nav`, `main`, `article`, and headings provide structure that browsers and assistive technology can expose. That usually means less JavaScript and ARIA to recreate behavior. Semantic structure also gives search engines and other tools clearer content signals. CSS can change the visual presentation without changing the meaning. I would start with the correct HTML element, keep the source order logical, and only build a custom control when native HTML cannot express the interaction. ```html caption="Use elements whose native meaning matches the content or action."

Release notes

```

question.en: A teammate adds role="button" and an onclick handler to a div and calls it done. Is it?

answer.en: No. The role only changes how the element is mapped in the accessibility tree; it adds no behavior. The div is still not focusable, does not activate on Enter or Space, and lacks every other native button behavior, so tabindex, key handlers, and state must be hand-built. That is exactly the JavaScript and ARIA a native button gives you for free, which is why the default is the correct HTML element.

question.en: A design shows a whole card as clickable, with a title, an image, and a secondary link inside. How do you build it without wrecking semantics?

answer.en: Keep the card a non-interactive container and make its primary action a real link or button whose hit area covers the card via CSS, while the secondary action stays a separate real control. CSS can stretch the primary control's presentation without changing the meaning of the markup. Building a custom control is the last resort, for when native HTML cannot express the interaction.

question.en: How would you structure a page so users can navigate its regions and headings?

answer.en: I would give the document one clear primary `main` region, use `nav` for navigation, `header` and `footer` where their scope is meaningful, and use headings to describe the content hierarchy. I would make heading levels reflect the outline rather than choose them for font size. Landmark labels should distinguish repeated regions when there is more than one of the same type. The source order should make sense without CSS, because screen-reader reading order and keyboard traversal follow the document structure rather than the visual arrangement.

question.en: A page has a header navigation, a breadcrumb, and a footer navigation, all as nav elements. Screen-reader users hear 'navigation' three times. What do you do?

answer.en: Give repeated regions of the same type distinguishing labels, for example aria-label="Primary", "Breadcrumb", and "Footer" on each nav, so the landmark list shows three distinguishable entries and users can jump directly to the one they want.

question.en: A screen-reader user reports your page 'jumps from heading level 1 to level 4'. The visual design uses three font sizes that do not map to h2, h3, h4. What went wrong and what do you change?

answer.en: Heading levels were chosen to match the mockup's font sizes instead of the document outline. Fix the markup so levels reflect the actual content hierarchy, and restyle the sizes in CSS. Also re-check the source order, because screen-reader reading order follows the document, not the visual arrangement.

question.en: What makes a form control accessible, and why is a placeholder not a label?

answer.en:
Each control needs a durable accessible name, normally from a visible `label` associated with its `id` and the label's `for`. The label tells users what information belongs in the control and increases the clickable target. A placeholder is only a hint: it disappears when typing and should not carry the control's identifying purpose. For related radio buttons or checkboxes, I would group them with `fieldset` and `legend`. I would also use the appropriate input type and native constraints, then provide clear instructions and errors.

```html caption="An explicit label association gives the control a stable name."
<label for="email">Email address</label>
<input id="email" name="email" type="email" autocomplete="email" required />
```

question.en: An input has a visible label reading 'Email address' and also aria-label="Contact email". Which name do screen readers announce, and why can that be a problem?

answer.en: They announce 'Contact email'. In the accessible name computation, aria-label takes precedence over an associated label element, so the visible label is replaced, not combined. Keep them consistent: WCAG 2.5.3 Label in Name expects the visible label text to be part of the accessible name, because speech-input users say what they see (https://www.w3.org/TR/accname-1.2/, https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/label-in-name.html).

question.en: The design marks required fields with a red asterisk only. How do you make 'required' perceivable without guessing?

answer.en: Expose it programmatically with the native required attribute (or aria-required for custom controls) so the state is announced, keep any visible convention like the asterisk explained in text near the top of the form or in the label, and never rely on color alone. Group related controls with fieldset and legend so radio and checkbox sets also announce their group context.

sources.label: MDN: Forms and buttons in HTML

question.en: How should client-side and server-side form validation work together?

answer.en: Client-side constraints such as `required`, an input `type`, and other validation attributes give fast feedback and prevent common formatting mistakes before submission. They are a usability feature, not a security boundary: a client can disable JavaScript or send a request directly. The server must validate and safely process every submitted value. Errors should be specific, visible, associated with the affected control, and not communicated by color alone. After a failed submission, preserve entered values where appropriate and make the error summary or first invalid field reachable without creating an unexpected focus jump.

question.en: The team wants to disable the submit button until every client-side constraint passes, to prevent invalid submissions. Why is that an accessibility problem?

answer.en: Disabled controls are not focusable and their state is not necessarily perceived or explained, so keyboard and screen-reader users can reach a silent dead end with no idea what is wrong. Keep the button enabled, validate on submission, and return specific, visible errors associated with each affected control. The server must validate everything anyway, because client-side constraints are a usability feature, not a security boundary.

question.en: Server validation fails and you render the errors client-side. How do you connect each message to its field?

answer.en: Keep the label as the field's name and attach the message text with aria-describedby so it is announced when the user focuses the field. Make errors visible, specific, and not communicated by color alone, and after a failed submission make an error summary or the first invalid field reachable without an unexpected focus jump, preserving the entered values.

question.en: Which HTML choices provide a sound SEO foundation?

answer.en:
I start with meaningful, crawlable content in the HTML: a descriptive document title, the correct language declaration, a logical heading hierarchy, descriptive link text, semantic sections, and useful text alternatives for meaningful images. Navigation should use real links with URLs, not clickable spans that only work after JavaScript runs. The page should remain understandable in source order and at different viewport sizes. These practices primarily improve structure, usability, and interpretation; they are not a promise of a ranking position. SEO basics and accessibility often align because both benefit from clear, honest document semantics. ```html caption="Clear metadata, language, headings, and link text form a solid HTML baseline." question.en: We replaced the divs with semantic elements and rankings did not move. Was the refactor pointless?

answer.en: No, but the expectation was wrong. Semantic markup is a foundation: it gives browsers, assistive technology, and other tools clearer content signals and usually improves usability and accessibility, which is why SEO basics and accessibility often align. It is not a promise of a ranking position, which depends on many factors outside your markup.

question.en: The marketing navigation is built from clickable spans wired up by JavaScript. Why does that hurt crawlers and screen-reader users alike?

answer.en: Real links with hrefs carry the semantics: a destination, keyboard and assistive-technology activation, and a crawlable URL. Span-based navigation only works after JavaScript runs, so the destinations are invisible to tools that do not execute it, and the keyboard and screen-reader affordances of a link are gone.

question.en: How would you design a responsive navigation that remains accessible when it collapses?

answer.en:
I would keep navigation as real links inside a `nav`, provide a native button to open and close the compact menu, and expose its state with `aria-expanded` and its controlled region with `aria-controls` when needed. The closed panel should not remain in the keyboard or accessibility tree. The toggle itself needs a clear name and visible focus. On open, focus management must be predictable; on close, return focus to the toggle if the user initiated the close. I test the full flow with keyboard, touch, zoom, narrow widths, and a screen reader, including the case where JavaScript is delayed or fails. ```html caption="The button exposes state; the links remain native navigation."
Docs
```

question.en: The user closes the mobile menu with Escape or its close button. Where should focus go?

answer.en: Back to the menu toggle, when the user initiated the close from inside the panel. Otherwise the focused element inside the now-hidden panel is removed, focus resets to the document start, and keyboard users must re-traverse the page to get back where they were. If focus is already outside the panel, leave it alone.

question.en: The collapsed panel is hidden by positioning it off-screen with left: -9999px instead of being truly hidden. What is the problem?

answer.en: Off-screen content stays in the accessibility tree and the tab order, so users tab through invisible links and hear a menu that is supposedly closed. Use the hidden attribute or display: none so the closed panel is actually removed from rendering, the tab order, and the accessibility tree.
